findings.issue: dueFor does not check the range of the event amounts. If returnItemsValue is negative, the share is negative. If returnItemsValue/orderItemsValue is very large, BigDecimal.intValue() keeps only the low-order bits, so the share can wrap to a negative or meaningless int. No ledger row is written in either case, because of the `> 0` guards. But the negative redeem_due/earn_due is stored in coin_return_reversals and lowers `prior`, so a later completing return computes remaining = total - prior > total and gives back more than N redeemed coins. Exploiting this needs a forged order.events message. order-service computes the value as the sum of positive unitPrice x quantity, so the normal path cannot produce it. It is still a ledger-integrity gap, because this change trusts two new amount fields from the payload.
findings.fix: Clamp the inputs and the result: return 0 if value.signum() < 0; use value.min(orderValue) before the multiply; take the result with intValueExact() or compare it against `remaining` while still a BigDecimal; return Math.max(0, Math.min(share, remaining)). Also guard total - prior so it never goes negative before it is written. A CHECK (redeem_due >= 0 AND earn_due >= 0 AND earn_taken >= 0 AND earn_taken <= earn_due) on V5 would enforce this in the database. Since V5 is not released yet, it can still be edited in this PR.

findings.issue: The legacy paths do not account for the new per-return rows. releaseRedeem (credits +N as redeem-<order>) and onFullyRefunded (earn-<order>) ignore coin_return_reversals. The new path counts legacy rows as prior, but not the other way round. Today releaseRedeem runs only on cancel or payment failure, which cannot follow a delivered and returned order, so it is not reachable. The design and runbook document the onFullyRefunded over-reversal on rollback; it hurts the customer, not the store. Any future caller of releaseRedeem on a post-delivery path would double-credit redeemed coins.
findings.fix: In releaseRedeem, subtract SUM(redeem_due) from coin_return_reversals for the order (or skip when rows exist). Or add a comment or assert that it must never run after a return refund. A one-line guard is cheap.

findings.issue: Redeemed coins given back on a return are inserted with expires_at NULL (never expire). A customer can redeem coins that are about to expire, return the items, and get the same coins back as non-expiring coins. releaseRedeem on cancel already behaves this way, so this is a small extension of existing behaviour, not a new class of abuse.
findings.fix: Accept and record it in the runbook, or give the give-back row the expiry of the coins originally redeemed (or the default expiry()).

findings.issue: coin_return_reversals holds user_id plus order and return amounts. It is kept on USER_DELETED, the same as coin_ledger, and PrivacyExportController does not include it. The table holds only pseudonymous UUIDs and integers, and the runbook records the backlog item, but the data-subject export is incomplete until that item is done.
findings.fix: Add the backlog item to docs/techdebt/README.md with an ID so it is tracked, not only mentioned in operations.md.

summary: No new HTTP endpoint, /internal route, dependency or secret is added. The SQL is fully parameterised; the only string concatenation in SQL selects between two fixed column names. Customer gain is controlled. A replayed or redelivered RETURN_REFUNDED is a no-op: it is checked against the return_id primary key under the per-user pg_advisory_xact_lock, and the ledger unique key is a second guard. Concurrent sibling returns serialise on the same user lock, and an event with a mismatched userId fails on the primary key and rolls back. The age-gate exemption covers only events that carry returnId and returnItemsValue, and replays are idempotent per return, so it reopens nothing. The listener branches are mutually exclusive, so onFullyRefunded and onReturnRefunded never both run on one event. Legacy redeem-/earn- rows count as prior. Floor rounding works against the customer on give-backs, and the completing return settles the exact remainder, with totals capped at N and E. There is no double dip between money and coins: Order.requestReturn already removes the coin share from the money refund pro rata, so the pro-rata coin give-back matches it. The spend-first clamp is the accepted CEO policy. The redeem give-back is applied before the clamp, so the customer cannot keep more than the shortfall. The shortfall is recorded every time (earn_due/earn_taken, including 0), it is idempotent after a clamp (tested), and it is logged with UUIDs only, no PII. The new trust from the Kafka payload is the two amounts returnItemsValue and orderItemsValue. The payload's userId was already trusted. The amounts are not range-checked, and a forged negative or overflowing value could write a negative due that inflates a later completing return's give-back. That needs write access to order.events, which already allows forging DELIVERED totals, so I rate it minor and recommend clamping plus a CHECK constraint. The other minors cover the asymmetry with the legacy releaseRedeem, non-expiring give-backs, and the missing privacy export. No blocker or major findings, so the verdict is approve.
